hints: For every prime dividing k, look at the exponent in each array element.
In each adjacent pair, at least one exponent must equal its exponent in k.
Count these independent exponent choices with a two-state recurrence.
analogy: For each prime, a fully powered position must cover every neighboring pair.
example: For n=3 and k=4, exponents 0,1,2 are allowed and no two neighboring exponents can both be below 2; there are 11 valid arrays.
algorithm: Factor k into prime powers p^e. For one prime, let F be the number of exponent sequences ending at e and L the number ending below e. Start at length 1 with F=1 and L=e. Extend by F_new=F+L and L_new=e*F. Compute the length-n state using 2 by 2 matrix exponentiation modulo 1000000007. Multiply F+L over all prime factors; if k=1, the answer is 1.
correctness: Each element must divide k. For a prime power p^e, the LCM condition holds on an edge exactly when at least one endpoint has exponent e. A below-e exponent has e choices and can only follow a full exponent; a full exponent can follow either state. Prime choices are independent, and unique factorization makes their product the number of arrays.
complexity: Trial division factors each k in O(sqrt(k)); if it has r distinct prime factors, matrix exponentiation takes O(r log n) time and O(1) extra space.
